qAndA.answer: Because SHA 256 produces unique outputs for every different input, this hash, created from his specific image, is highly likely to be the first and only instance of that number being generated.
qAndA.question: Why does the speaker call the hash generated from his snow globe picture a 'world premiere'?

qAndA.answer: Even a minor change, like changing a single bit in a file, will drastically alter the resulting SHA 256 hash, showcasing its sensitivity to input variations.
qAndA.question: What is the 'butterfly effect' in the context of SHA 256?

qAndA.answer: Bitcoin mining involves finding a specific input (a 'nonce') that, when combined with other block data and run through the SHA 256 algorithm, produces a hash output with a certain number of leading zeros.
qAndA.question: How is SHA 256 related to Bitcoin mining?

qAndA.answer: While computing the hash from an input is relatively straightforward, reversing the process and figuring out the original input from just the hash is incredibly difficult, if not impossible with current methods.
qAndA.question: What makes SHA 256 a 'one-way' function?

qAndA.answer: The speaker gets anxious after discovering that the NSA designed SHA 256. This revelation suggests potential hidden intentions or control over the widely used algorithm, leading to uneasiness and conspiracy theories.
qAndA.question: Why does the speaker become anxious at the end of the video?

youtube_description:
No one on Earth knows how to reverse one of the most popular computer algorithms. Yet it's really easy to compute one-way. You could make billions of dollars if you solved this mathematics problem, which is computed quintillions of times per second in the race for mining Bitcoin. SHA256 has some amazing properties, is useful for digital signatures, cryptography, authentication, and is a central part of the Bitcoin protocol.

(**** UPDATE 2021: After two years, I've finally posted a follow-up video, an introduction to Bitcoin. You can find it here: https://youtu.be/LzhJjSRad5A )

Bitcoin and other "crypto-currencies" rely on one-way hash functions like the SHA-256 algorithm to secure the blockchain where all the transactions are kept.

In this video, I explain some of the big-picture ideas behind this one function. Other cryptocurrencies use similar ideas.

Comments, suggestions, or errors? Let me know in the comments, and I'll fix them in an upcoming follow-up video.

Take a look at some of my other videos:  https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL625C69DF58409759
